author: Pip Hinman
title: Albanese’s United Nations climate hypocrisy
content:
Anthony Albanese’s speech to the United Nations during “climate week” revealed just how out of touch he and his government is with the widespread community concern over runaway climate change.

Albanese delivered a sort of homily in New York. He said scientists have “warned” us about climate change and that Australia “understands the dangers of global warming and the urgency of climate action”.

He went on to praise firefighters and special emergency service workers for showing the “best of humanity” in the 2019-20 Black Summer bushfire crises and various devastating floods.

With hand on heart, Albanese said: “There’s no avoiding the scale of our responsibility — or the cost of inaction”, before going on to praise Australians for “choosing to electrify” with “clean, reliable, more affordable energy”.

While rooftop solar energy powers at least 13% of our energy, and Australia is on track to meet its rooftop solar targets, it is a wrong to argue, as Albanese essentially did, that the climate can be “saved” by individual households choosing to go green.

As long as the big polluters — fossil fuel corporations — continue to be subsidised by govenrments, climate change will worsen. The Climate Council has done the research and said the big polluters are expected to reduce their share by just 7.6% over the five years to 2030, compared to a 19% reduction across the rest of the count

author: Renfrey Clarke
title: Whyalla Steel sackings show need for public ownership
content:
The firm of administrators charged with selling the Whyalla Steelworks plant in South Australia announced on September 14 that efforts to repair the plant’s blast furnace had been abandoned. Smelting of iron ore would cease and of the plant’s total of close to 1700 regular workers, some 500 would lose their jobs.

Joining them would be about 100 “labour hire” workers and many of the 200 “embedded contractors” working at the plant but employed by other companies.

It is hard to overstate the impact of the sackings on Whyalla and its 21,000 people. It is thought that about five further local jobs are to be created from the spending of each full-time steelworks employee. A huge chunk of money will thus be gouged out of the city’s narrowly-based economy. Small businesses will shut their doors, and property values will crash.

One of many ironies is that demand for the steel plant’s main products remains strong.

Whyalla, in recent years, has produced about three-quarters of Australia’s structural steel and all of the country’s output of “long products” such as steel rails and girders. Production of these goods will continue, with the plant’s rolling mill processing imports of semi-finished steel “blooms”. Also carrying on will be production — now for shipment elsewhere — of smelter-ready iron ore pellets, on the basis of the ore resources of the nearby Middleback Range.

author: John Mullen
title: Will the French have a fascist president next May? Questions and answers about the far right in France today
content:
The upcoming French presidential election next May carries weight far beyond France’s borders.

A victory for fascist candidate Marine Le Pen — in a major world economy — would embolden far-right movements globally while dealing a terrible blow to French workers, particularly women, LGBT+ people and Muslims.

Conversely, a win for the radical left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, of the France Insoumise (France in Revolt, FI)[1] would offer an important boost to anti-capitalists everywhere.

This election will be anything but business as usual. A recent poll revealed that 71% of voters want the new president to bring about “real social and political change”.[2]

This Q and A aims to explain the key dynamics at work, as well as the strengths and weaknesses of antifascist activity in France today.

Will the French have a fascist president next May?

Nobody can know the answer to this question right now, but the danger is very real. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen of the Rassemblement National (National Rally, RN) is the favourite in the polls, with around 33% of voting intentions for the first round.[3] No other candidate polls above 20%.

Le Pen has particularly gained ground in recent years among women voters[4] and public sector workers, traditionally populations where the left is strong.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Socialist Alliance NSW calls for moratorium on AI mega data centres
content:
Socialist Alliance NSW said it wholeheartedly supports community calls for a moratorium on the construction of artificial intelligence mega data centres.

“The expansion of mega data centres in Australia is mostly unregulated. Many of the industrial sites slated for mega data centres are right next to residential areas,” Isaac Nellist who is standing for Socialist Alliance in Balmain, told Green Left.

There are 47 artificial intelligence (AI) mega data centres being planned in NSW, including 20 State Significant Developments and 15 key projects.

“These mega data centres mostly use excessive water and energy and are likely to destabilise local supplies. We note that the Victorian government has moved to quell legitimate community anxiety about the rapid construction of these mega data centres.

“It says it will ‘set the rules’, including that they must use their own renewable energy supply and storage, meet connection costs and network upgrades and use recycled or non-drinking water for cooling.

“But another key issue is where these constructions are sited: Victorian Labor has promised a ‘buffer’ between homes and data centres — but of only 150 metres. This will not allay community concerns about noise and other pollution.”

Socialist Alliance also shares community concerns about what these centres are being used for.

author: Susan Price
title: Campaign to name and shame companies fuelling Indonesia’s wildfire crisis
content:
An escalating wildfire crisis in Indonesia since July has covered much of Southeast Asia in a protracted and hazardous smoke haze.

Greenpeace Malaysia and Himpunan Advocacy Rakyat Malaysia (HARAM) held a peaceful protest outside the Indonesian embassy in Malaysia’s capital, Kuala Lumpur, on September 4, in solidarity with all communities affected by the cross-border haze and the loss of wildlife, suffered most severely in Indonesia.

The protesters did not blame Indonesians for the crisis but, instead called for the corporate interests that are complicit in the crisis — including Malaysian companies — to be named and shamed.

"While corporate executives sit comfortably in their air-conditioned offices earning millions of dollars in profit, it is the common citizens, workers, students and even the children of Malaysia and Indonesia who are breathing in and dying from the haze. Schools are closing down, and our basic human right to breathe is being taken away from us. Clean air doesn’t have a passport, nor does environmental devastation. We stand firmly in solidarity with the communities in Indonesia who are affected by these fires,” HARAM chairman Brendon Gan said in a statement.

author: Pip Hinman
title: We need to stand up against genocide
content:
Cathy Eatock gave the following speech to the International Day of Peace rally on September 20 on Gadigal Country, organised by Sydney Anti-AUKUS Coalition and Stop the War on Palestine.

AUKUS ties us irrevocably to the United States war machine.

Australia has previously blindly followed the US into the war on terror which led to the deaths of an estimated 4.7 million people in Iraq, Syria and Libya.

Now the Anthony Albanese government has, astoundingly, followed Scott Morrison into AUKUS, without question or public discussion. The obscene cost of $368 billion over 30 years means hospitals, aged care homes, housing, education, the National Disability Support Scheme, dental and mental health services, and Aboriginal communities won’t receive the funding we need.

With each submarine having its own nuclear reactor, its radioactive waste will need to be stored here.

But Aboriginal people have repeatedly rejected even low-grade medical uranium waste being stored on their lands. The Aboriginal communities of Maralinga, Emu plain and Montebello Islands have already borne the brunt of nuclear testing.

Pacific peoples in the Marshall Islands, Christmas Island, French Polynesia and Kiribati have endured 315 nuclear weapons tests. It is the Pacific and Aboriginal communities that continues to suffer that legacy.

author: Sue Bolton
title: Labor must stop helping One Nation scapegoat migrants
content:
Home affairs and immigration minister Tony Burke’s speech to the National Press Club (NPC) on September 17 was a boost to Pauline Hanson’s One Nation and its Trumpite politics of hate, racism and division.

Burke’s speech, delayed for a month, was always framed as Labor’s “new” plan to get tougher on immigration.

It was a blatant concession to One Nation’s billionaire-funded campaign to scapegoat recent and non-European migrants for the housing and cost-of-living crisis, despite them being a result of the establishment parties’ neoliberal policies since the 1980s.

This bipartisan approach is responsible for making housing totally unaffordable for a new generation of workers. It has reduced real wages and eroded basic social rights, including the right to public health, education, transport and welfare.

Migrant workers are not the cause of these problems. However, with the backing of Gina Rinehart, Australia’s wealthiest billionaire, Hanson has whipped up a panic about “mass migration”; it is her way way of shifting the blame from the billionaire class to the most vulnerable sections of the working class.

Burke said that One Nation’s claims about “mass migration” were “absurd” and “not something we're dealing with in Australia”. But he went on to outline measures to cut net overseas migration from 290,000 to 225,000, in 2027-28, and make life harder for migrant workers and i

author: Susan Price
title: ‘Ecological crisis creates a challenge and an opportunity for the left’
content:
Ayesha Ahmad, a Pakistani socialist-feminist activist, researcher, educator, and labour rights practitioner with the Haqooq-e-Khalq Party, was one of the guest speakers at the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13. She spoke to Green Left’s Peter Boyle about the impact of the mounting global ecological crisis on politics in Pakistan.

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal as a result of global warming and the melting of the Himalayan glaciers were a warning to the world, but does it have a special significance for Pakistan, which also borders the Himalayas?

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal are a profound warning for Pakistan. For years, Pakistan has been among the countries most exposed to the climate crisis in South Asia, and we have already witnessed what a warming Himalaya can do — from the catastrophic 2022 floods, to increasingly frequent glacial lake outburst floods in Gilgit-Baltistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The Nepal disaster tells us that we may be entering an even more dangerous phase of the Himalayan climate crisis.

But for me, there is a much deeper question here. South Asia shares a history. We share the history of colonial extraction, of loot and plunder, of resources being taken from our lands to build wealth elsewhere. author: Susan Price
title: Timor-Leste’s struggle for freedom and the politics of refugee protection
content:
The Good Sea: The Journey of the ‘Tasi Diak’ and the Politics of Refugee Protection in Australia By Vannessa Hearman Melbourne University Press (2026) 256pp. $36.99

A small boat set out from occupied East Timor (Timor-Leste), bound for Darwin on May 24, 1995. On board were 17 activists who had been campaigning against the Indonesian occupation of their homeland, as well as a six-month-old baby.

Some of the passengers had participated in protests that had been violently repressed by the Indonesian army. Some had given support to the guerrilla resistance fighters in the mountains. Now, they wanted to take the case for Timor-Leste’s independence to the people of Australia and the world.

The Good Sea: The Journey of the ‘Tasi Diak’ and the Politics of Refugee Protection in Australia tells the story of their voyage and their experiences before and after.

Author Vannessa Hearman, born in Indonesia and based at Curtin University in Western Australia, is a historian of Southeast Asia, specialising in political violence, human rights and historical memory in Indonesia and Timor-Leste.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Students walk out of class again to protest Hanson’s racism and bigotry
content:
Thousands of high school and university students again walked out of class a second time to protest Pauline Hanson’s racism and bigotry on September 17. Rallies were held in 18 cities and towns across the country.

Students highlighted Hanson’s racist comments towards First Nations people and immigrants, her anti-LGBTIQ stance, her claim that domestic violence is a “two-way street” and her denial of the climate crisis.

Many pointed out that Hanson’s claim to be representing “ordinary Australians” is shown to be a lie because she is backed by Gina Rinehart, Australia’s richest person, and has consistently voted against pay rises and improved workers’ rights.

Students at the rally in Gadigal Country/Sydney told Green Left they did not support the vision for the country that Hanson is putting forward. “We’re the next generation of voters and we don’t want to see people like Pauline Hanson and One Nation who spread bigotry and hate in power,” one student said.

A year-12 student told Green Left he attended the protest to oppose Hanson’s racist rhetoric, and its adoption by Labor and the Coalition. “I’m here to stand in solidarity with women, immigrants, Palestinians, Indigenous people and queer people.”

Another student said they want politicians who are “for the people and not for billionaires”. “My mum is a person of colour and we don’t want someone who’s going to be racist.”

author: Pip Hinman
title: Socialist Alliance trade unionists to contest Western Victoria Region
content:
Socialist Alliance in Victoria has announced candidates for the Legislative Council in the Western Victoria Region at the November 28 elections.

The party is running on the campaign theme of “Fighting for people, not the billionaires”.

Tim Gooden, Sue Bull and Ross Smith are active trade unionists from the construction and maritime industries, and think progressive working class people need to be heard.

Gooden, a former Secretary of Geelong Trades Hall and a Palestine justice campaigner, told Green Left: “We are putting forward positive solutions for workers rather than the hate which is being put out by the big end of town. Blaming migrants and refugees for cost-of-living rises is about scapegoating people who have nothing. Meanwhile, the billionaires rake in profits.”

Bull, a teacher trainer in schools and the construction industry for many years told GL: “State and federal governments can always find money to subsidise their big business mates, but when it comes to funding housing, health or education, the coffers are bare. We need to build a movement that fights for us and our needs.”

author: Pip Hinman
title: Ecosocialism 2026 forges unity and builds struggles
content:
“The big people behind capitalism are quite aware that they are planning the end of the world as we know it”, Sabrina Fernandes, a political economist and ecosocialist activist from Brazil, told the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13.

“They don’t have a problem with the world ending as we know it — as long as they can keep making profits,” Fernandes said.

“They do have a problem with a society that they might not be able to control when things get really hard, as we are coming to this stage of ecocide and global catastrophe. They are fighting over the spoils of war and climate change.”

Places that would not normally be considered part of the grab are becoming so, Fernandes said. The oceans “are a new terra nullius for them” — for ocean floor mining.

There should be an international agreement for this, but US President Donald Trump does not care and has begun issuing his own licences, she added.

Helen Yaffe, author, activist and Professor of Latin American Political Economy, University of Glasgow, told the conference that socialist Cuba, one of the key targets of Trump’s new colonialism, is facing multiple and mounting challenges as the US blockade intensifies.

The response that she has witnessed, in a recent visit to Cuba, was: “We shall not submit!”

author: Susan Price
title: ‘The Return’ uses magical realism to confront Israel’s genocide
content:
Jordan Shukri AK Armaou-Massoud

The Return Written and directed by Ala’a Al Qaisi Touring Sydney, Melbourne and regional Victoria Visit thereturnproject.com.au for details

Green Left’s Jordan Shukri AK Armaou-Massoud caught up with award-winning Palestinian writer director Ala’a Al Qaisi about her play, The Return, which has been touring Sydney, Melbourne and regional Victoria since September 1.

“As war tears through Gaza, a father waits for the clouds to bring his daughters home.”

So reads the synopsis for The Return, a powerfully surreal stage play written and directed by award-winning Palestinian writer director Ala’a Al Qaisi.

Al Qaisi told Green Left her idea for the play started early into Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinians, when she saw a video of a father from Gaza whose name is Marwan Abu Samra.

Marwan was in a hospital next to his daughter Nagham — a famous karate champion who represented Palestine whenever she could leave Gaza to travel. Nagham’s leg had been amputated and she was in a coma — the result of an Israeli airstrike.

“[Marwan] already lost Rozan, his other daughter, in the same strike, and he was cleaving to the wall to help him get Nagham out of Gaza to get treatment because, at the time, they didn’t even have any antibiotics to save her,” Al Qaisi said.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Big data and the AUKUS war machine
content:
The world’s greatest remilitarisation since the World War II is underway, driven by the imperatives of the flailing United States empire.

The AUKUS war pact places us at the centre of this drive towards war. How should we imagine Australia’s role in the world?

Australia is not just a settler-colonial state; it is a sub-imperial power that has transferred subordination from its one-time colonial ruler, Britain, to the US, its new imperial master.

It is now acting to preserve the military and economic interests of its master state. This is encapsulated in the AUKUS war pact, which, despite no public debate, commits the country to eight nuclear-powered submarines, high-tech weapons development and sharing and the subsequent invasion of US personnel and weaponry in the event of our “interoperability” in a contrived future conflict with China.

Through AUKUS, Australia acts as a mechanism for US force projection into the Pacific, to rattle the sabre against China.

AUKUS makes Australia the first non-nuclear-weapons state to use a loophole in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons for naval propulsion with weapons-grade uranium.

That sets a proliferation precedent.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Greens divided over koala park carbon credit scam
content:
Federal Labor has maintained its unwavering support for the fossil fuel industry against persistent community demands for genuine climate action by voting down a disallowance motion that would have blocked the so-called Improved Native Forest Management (INFM) system.

Controversially, seven of 10 Australian Greens Senators voted with Labor on September 10. But Greens Senators Nick McKim, Jordon Steele-John and Vanessa Bleyer supported the motion, although not because they agreed with the Nationals-One Nation movers.

The WA Greens MPs said that they “strongly opposed” the INFM method and were “disappointed” that colleagues voted with Labor, “thereby allowing the INFM method to remain in place”. They said the INFM system could generate 1.5 million carbon credits.

Supporters of the Labor-Green deal say it will save koalas and forest habitat.

Greens leader Larissa Waters said: “These improvements will help deliver the Great Koala National Park (GKNP) in NSW, protecting 176,000 hectares of native forest and safeguarding habitat for around 12,000 koalas and more than 100 other threatened species”.

However, it also means that saving forests and koalas relies on creating new carbon credits in an already dodgy carbon trading market.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Activists face charges in Singapore
content:
Anti-death penalty activists Jolovan Wham and Elijah Tay faced court on September 7 and 9, charged with 19 offences under Singapore’s Public Order Act and Penal Code.

Tay, who is also a campaigner in solidarity with Palestinians against Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, participated in the Ecosocialism 2024 conference in Boorloo/Perth.

Tay is being charged with: participating in candlelight vigils for death row inmates; participating in a photo outside the state court where people had their fists raised and were all wearing “not in my name” t-shirts in solidarity with people sentenced to death; organising a shoe memorial for children martyred in Gaza outside an Israeli-linked research building at Singapore’s national university; participating in a walk to the Ministry of Home Affairs to deliver feedback about a proposed government law that would be detrimental to free speech; chanting “from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” at a private indoor assembly livestreamed on social media; and for not answering a public servant (likely a police officer) during questioning.

Wham, who is an anti-death penalty activist, is also being charged with participating in a candlelight vigil for death row inmates; organising an assembly outside the state courts; and not answering a public servant during questioning, among other charges.

author: Susan Price
title: ‘We can all have a good life and live within planetary boundaries’
content:
See Yong Feng was one of the guest speakers at the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane on September 11–13. He explained in his presentation, “Degrowth and Ecosocialism”, how it would be possible for all people — in the Global South and Global North — to have a good life without crossing planetary boundaries.

See previously worked as an architect and returned to Singapore last year after completing a Masters in political ecology, environmental justice and degrowth at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. He currently works in book publishing and organises with Singapore Climate Rally as well as the independent media network NIMBUS.

During the conference, See spoke with Green Left’s Peter Boyle about degrowth and how humanity can live within planetary boundaries.

You studied under Professor Jason Hickel at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. He has been at the cutting edge of debates and discussions around ecosocialism and degrowth. What do you think are the most important areas of research that Hickel and his team have covered in the past couple of years?

Research has been done to quantify and prove to conventional economists — and other people who need to see the facts — the extent of the extraction and exploitation that’s going on.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Join International Day of Peace protests to scrap AUKUS, stop war on Gaza
content:
Anti-war and solidarity groups are protesting across the country, September 12–21, to demand an end to the war alliance with the United States and for AUKUS to be scrapped.

September 15 also marks the fifth anniversary of the Coalition government signing the AUKUS Pillar I and II pact with the US and Britain. Labor adopted AUKUS as its own and has refused to support a parliamentary inquiry.

New publicly released data shows that the US military and weapons corporations control, or have unimpeded access, to more than 100 military facilities across Australia. More than half of the military facilities in this country are controlled, or used extensively, by the US military, in preparation for a major war.

AUKUS is supposedly costing upwards of $368 billion over the next 30 years. That means some $35 million a day is being siphoned away from health, education, affordable housing and many urgent social needs to fund wars of aggression and weapons corporations.

As the US and Israel make the world a more dangerous place, Labor continues to give its support to both, including by sending weapons parts to Israel for its F-35 fighter jet parts.

Australia also supplies intelligence through the Pine Gap spy base in central Australia, which can be used by Israel to pinpoint targets.
